strengths: The checklist formulation is clear, practical, and well motivated: decomposing broad criteria into binary decisions directly targets ambiguity in holistic Likert judging while providing an auditable breakdown of the resulting score.

The empirical study is broad, covering 12 open- and closed-weight evaluators of several sizes, two principal NLG benchmarks, and an additional factual-consistency benchmark. CheckEval generally improves human correlation and is substantially less sensitive to evaluator choice, including for several smaller models.

The paper commendably distinguishes human alignment from inter-evaluator reliability and includes useful controls and analyses: two agreement coefficients, binarized G-Eval outputs, increased baseline sampling, component ablations, question weighting, quality-stratified results, and human-curated filtering.

Human studies assess both checklist construction and direct human use of the protocol. The released code, full prompts, seed questions, model identifiers, inference settings, hardware, and API costs provide a reasonably strong basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central inter-evaluator-agreement comparison is insufficiently specified and may not measure comparable objects. CheckEval's identical alpha and kappa values strongly suggest agreement is computed over individual binary question answers, whereas G-Eval and SEEval are assessed using one holistic dimension rating. Agreement on many narrow questions does not establish agreement between the final aggregated scores; binarizing a holistic baseline score does not equalize the observational unit. Continuous/ordinal agreement or ICC on normalized final scores is needed, alongside an explicit derivation of the claimed average 0.45 improvement.

The main performance differences lack uncertainty estimates or paired significance tests. Several correlation advantages are small or reverse for particular models and dimensions, yet raw correlations are averaged across dimensions and heterogeneous models without confidence intervals or Fisher transformation. The variance/KDE analysis uses only 12 model-level correlations and measures variance in human alignment, not the abstract's stated variance of evaluation scores.

End-to-end robustness remains unclear because all conclusions condition on one benchmark-specific checklist produced from manually selected sub-dimensions and a single GPT-4o augmentation/filtering pipeline. There is no evaluation across independent checklist designers, generation models, or generation runs, nor a genuinely held-out task. Unequal numbers of augmented questions also implicitly and arbitrarily weight sub-dimensions under uniform question averaging.

The human validation is too limited for the strongest validity claims: the correlation study uses only 20 summaries, agreement is tested only for relevance, and kappa values of 0.53 for humans and 0.49 for humans plus LLMs are moderate rather than clearly high. The paper does not provide confidence intervals or sufficiently explain correlation aggregation, annotator training, or adjudication. It also states that 100 summaries on a 26-question relevance checklist require about 10,000 answers per annotator, although this setup implies roughly 2,600.

The claimed explainability benefit is demonstrated only through one favorable case study; binary answers expose intermediate decisions but are not necessarily faithful explanations. Practical cost is also incompletely controlled, since CheckEval elicits 20–35 decisions per dimension while the baselines emit one rating, and the inference-budget control is restricted to one model/dataset setting. These limitations, together with the narrow summarization/dialogue task coverage, keep the paper just below a confident main-conference recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important weakness of LLM-based evaluation with a simple, interpretable checklist formulation whose aggregate score is traceable to specific binary judgments.

The empirical scope is strong: 12 open- and closed-weight evaluators of several sizes, two main benchmarks plus QAGS, and multiple correlation measures. CheckEval often improves human correlation, especially for weaker evaluators, and produces less cross-model variation in correlation.

The manuscript includes useful ablations and analyses concerning filtering, augmentation, weighting, output binarization, inference sampling, text-quality strata, and human application of the checklist.

Implementation details, prompts, checkpoint links, question counts, costs, and a public code link support reproducibility, while the limitations section is unusually candid. The complete manuscript was inspected: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-hs7zjlz2/call-14f682e87fb9416b939504c4bba0d69a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central inter-evaluator-agreement comparison is insufficiently specified and appears not to compare the same measurement unit: CheckEval agreement is seemingly computed over individual binary question responses, whereas baseline agreement is over one holistic multi-category rating. Krippendorff's alpha and Fleiss' kappa are sensitive to category structure and prevalence; thresholding the holistic G-Eval rating does not resolve the difference in granularity. Reliability should be evaluated directly on the final aggregate scores using measures such as ICC, pairwise score error, and score correlation.

The claimed reduction in “score variance” is unsupported: Table 15 measures variance across models' correlations with human judgments, not variance among their scores for the same examples. Likewise, the abstract's claimed 0.45 average agreement improvement is not clearly derivable from the reported comparisons.

Main performance differences lack confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or source-blocked bootstrap analyses. Several gains for strong models are small or reverse for particular dimensions, so point estimates do not establish the manuscript's repeated claims of significant or consistent improvement.

CheckEval obtains dozens of binary decisions and substantially finer score resolution, while G-Eval generally supplies one 3- or 5-level judgment. This confounds decomposition with inference budget, ensembling, and reduced ties in rank correlation. The n=3 experiment covers only one evaluator and dataset and does not demonstrate matched token, call, or score-resolution budgets.

Evidence for the automated construction pipeline is weak. Augmentation and filtering yield only small ablation gains, and filtering removes almost no questions in most dimensions. Human validation evaluates retained-question quality rather than both retained and rejected questions, so it cannot measure filtering recall. Uniformly averaging questions also implicitly weights subdimensions according to how many variants GPT-4o generated.

Human validation is narrow: only 20 SummEval summaries support the correlation analysis, and agreement uses 100 summaries but only relevance. Human kappa of 0.53 and human-plus-LLM kappa of 0.49 are moderate rather than clearly high. The stated approximately 10,000 decisions per annotator is also inconsistent with 100 summaries times the 26 relevance questions reported in Table 17.

Generality remains uncertain because the main evidence covers summarization and one knowledge-grounded dialogue benchmark, while QAGS is another summarization-consistency dataset. The manually designed, benchmark-specific criteria are not evaluated on a held-out task or with a new checklist constructed independently of the evaluation benchmark.

The closest decompositional approaches, particularly HD-Eval, are not included in a controlled reliability comparison. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate what is contributed specifically by binary checklists versus established fine-grained criteria decomposition.

Decomposed yes/no judgments can expose which criteria drive a score and are easier to inspect than a single holistic rating. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-or7ksvko/call-507e06a8f07b4c7da88171cfa9477480/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluator sweep is substantial: 12 open and proprietary models spanning several sizes, two main benchmarks, and an additional QAGS experiment. CheckEval generally preserves or improves correlation with human scores across models.

The paper usefully looks beyond human correlation by considering cross-model behavior, and includes per-model and per-dimension results, ablations, weighting and binarization analyses, inference-budget analysis, and human validation.
The exposition is generally clear, and the released-code link, open-model identifiers, prompts, costs, and license information provide a reasonable starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is that the headline inter-evaluator-agreement comparison is not established on a clearly comparable unit. CheckEval's alpha/kappa apparently operate over many binary question judgments, while G-Eval and SEEval provide one holistic Likert judgment per sample and dimension. Kappa is sensitive to label space and prevalence; binarizing the holistic baseline does not equalize decomposition, number of judgments, or score resolution. Agreement on the final aggregated scalar scores—using an appropriate ICC, concordance, rank-agreement, or absolute-error analysis—is not reported. Moreover, Table 15 measures variance of correlations across models, not the claimed variance of evaluation scores.

The comparison changes several factors simultaneously: decomposition, binary response format, 20–35 judgments per dimension, quasi-continuous aggregation, prompt structure, and inference budget. The paper therefore cannot attribute gains to the checklist mechanism. A matched factorial comparison and a controlled decompositional baseline such as HD-Eval are needed; sampling G-Eval three times for one model and dataset is inadequate.

Claims of significant and consistent improvement lack paired bootstrap tests or confidence intervals. Several advantages are small or reverse for particular models and dimensions. Averaging correlations without uncertainty also ignores dependence among outputs from the same documents and generation systems.

Human validation is too limited for the broad claims: correlation uses only 20 summaries, and agreement uses only relevance on 100 summaries, yielding a moderate human kappa of 0.53. Aggregation, statistical tests, annotator independence, and the power analysis are insufficiently documented. The statement that each annotator answered about 10,000 relevance questions conflicts with 100 summaries times the reported 26-question relevance checklist, which equals 2,600.

Uniformly averaging LLM-generated questions gives sub-dimensions with more generated or redundant questions greater implicit weight. Filtering removes no questions for several dimensions and has essentially no ablation effect. The complete final checklists are absent from the manuscript, augmentation prompts retain unspecified placeholders, and exact proprietary-model snapshots, parsing failures, and seed values are not documented.

Generalization remains narrow: the main evidence covers task-specific checklists for short-form summarization and dialogue, with factual consistency relegated to the appendix. There is no held-out task or domain testing checklist construction from scratch. Likewise, a single selected case study does not validate the stronger explainability claim, since binary outputs identify decisions but provide no rationale. These concerns require new controlled experiments and clearer reporting, supporting resubmission next cycle rather than Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP meta-evaluation problem. Decomposing broad criteria into binary checks is intuitive and makes evaluation outputs more diagnostically useful than a single holistic score.

The empirical scope is substantial: 12 open- and closed-weight judges, several model sizes, two main tasks, and an additional QAGS study. CheckEval improves correlation with human judgments in most model–dataset combinations, including sizable gains for some weaker judges.

The evaluation considers cross-model agreement in addition to human correlation and includes useful ablations, per-dimension results, high-/low-quality analyses, a binarized-baseline control, and an inference-budget experiment.
Human studies, released code, prompts, seed questions, hardware and cost information, and a candid limitations section improve transparency.
weaknesses: The central inter-evaluator-agreement analysis is insufficiently specified. The paper does not clearly state whether the unit is an aggregate text-level score or an individual checklist response, which measurement level Krippendorff’s α uses, or how continuous checklist proportions are converted for Fleiss’ κ. The exact equality of α and κ for CheckEval alongside their large divergence for baselines suggests that methods may be evaluated using materially different representations. Binarizing one holistic G-Eval rating does not establish agreement of CheckEval’s final aggregate scores. Consequently, the headline reliability improvement, including the claimed gain of 0.45, is not presently auditable.

No confidence intervals or paired significance tests support the claimed correlation and agreement improvements, although many differences are small. Correlations also appear to ignore document/system clustering, and the post-hoc Top-3 analysis selects different judges for different methods on the evaluation data.

The checklists are manually tailored to each benchmark and evaluated on those same benchmarks. There is no held-out task-level evaluation or robustness analysis across seed writers, checklist-generation models, prompt/order variants, or repeated stochastic runs. QAGS adds another factual-summarization setting but little domain diversity, so claims about general NLG reliability are too broad.

Human validation remains limited: the correlation study uses only 20 summaries; agreement is tested only for relevance; combining humans and LLMs into one six-rater κ does not directly measure cross-group agreement; and checklist-quality validation relies on raw exact match under a strongly yes-skewed distribution. Same-protocol human–LLM correlation also provides weaker evidence of external validity than comparison against independently elicited judgments.

CheckEval uses roughly 20–35 customized decisions per dimension, whereas the primary baseline produces one holistic rating. The n=3 experiment for one model and dataset is not a matched token/compute control, and the implementation does not clarify whether G-Eval’s probability-weighted scoring is retained. End-to-end checklist-construction cost is also omitted.

Uniform averaging implicitly weights sub-dimensions according to how many questions augmentation happens to generate, while the checklist-quality study does not establish coverage or discriminativeness. Moreover, binary answers expose the model’s assertions but not their evidence or faithfulness, so the stronger explainability claim is supported only by a single illustrative case.

The reported “variance” is variance of model-level correlations, not per-input score variance or test–retest stability. Together with the unresolved agreement methodology, this prevents a clear Findings recommendation despite the promising idea and extensive experiments.

strengths: The paper targets an important, underexamined problem: reliability across LLM judges, not merely correlation with human scores. The checklist formulation is simple, intuitive, and makes individual judgments more auditable.

The evaluation covers 12 open- and closed-weight models of several sizes. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and the supplementary QAGS evaluation, CheckEval generally improves or preserves correlation with human judgments, including substantial gains for some weaker judges.

The paper includes useful ablations and controls concerning augmentation, filtering, question weighting, output binarization, and inference budget, alongside human studies of checklist generation and application.

The manuscript is generally clear and discloses model identifiers, prompts, question counts, costs, hardware, and a code link. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-y1f69vvi/call-b6e10cf11a7542b9aa17822263492340/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is that the central inter-evaluator-agreement analysis is insufficiently defined and may not be comparable across methods. The paper does not specify the rated units or Krippendorff-alpha measurement level. Fleiss kappa is categorical, whereas CheckEval's final scores are proportions. If agreement is instead computed over individual binary checklist answers—as the identical alpha and kappa values suggest—this compares many question-level judgments against one holistic Likert judgment, rather than comparing the reliability of the final metric scores. Post-hoc binarization of G-Eval does not correct this mismatch. Agreement should be reported directly on final per-example scores using an appropriate coefficient such as ICC or clearly specified interval alpha, with confidence intervals.

CheckEval simultaneously changes criterion decomposition, prompt specificity, number of decisions, score resolution, and computational budget. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate whether gains arise from binary answers, decomposition, richer task-specific criteria, or averaging 20–35 decisions. A matched factorial comparison—such as holistic binary, decomposed Likert, and decomposed binary protocols with comparable token budgets—is needed for the causal claims.

Most reported improvements are raw differences between dependent correlations, without paired tests or confidence intervals. Several advantages are small or reverse for particular models and dimensions. The KDE and variance analysis uses only 12 model-level correlations and measures variance of correlations, not the claimed variance of evaluation scores; it therefore does not establish score stability.

Human validation is too limited for the broad validity claims: checklist correlation uses only 20 summaries, and agreement is evaluated only for SummEval relevance. The reported human kappa of 0.53 and combined human/LLM kappa of 0.49 are moderate rather than clearly high. Testing whether correlations are nonzero does not show that CheckEval significantly outperforms the original human protocol.

Checklist content validity remains uncertain. Uniform question averaging gives greater weight to subdimensions that happened to receive more augmented questions, and the weighting ablation does not test equal weighting across subdimensions. Some seed criteria overlap dimensions, while the Topical-Chat groundedness seeds largely assess conversational relevance and consistency rather than explicit support from the supplied fact. The checklist-quality study assesses retained-question acceptability but not coverage or valid questions mistakenly removed.

Generalization and reproducibility are incomplete. The main evidence concerns short English summarization and dialogue outputs, with QAGS adding another summarization setting, so claims about diverse open-ended or long-form NLG are premature. The final augmented checklists are absent from the manuscript, prompt templates retain unspecified placeholders, the GPT-4o snapshot and parsing/retry rules are not given, and comparative token cost or latency is not reported. The manual seed-design requirement also limits the claimed scalability.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important NLP problem: LLM judges can correlate with humans while remaining inconsistent across evaluator models. CheckEval's decomposition into concrete Boolean questions is intuitive, practically relevant, and clearly presented. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-elnzev2s/call-ff5c8229ced648008352ecb622ff720d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 12 open- and closed-weight judges of several sizes, two main benchmarks, and QAGS in the appendix. CheckEval often improves human correlation, with particularly substantial gains for several weaker evaluators, although the advantage is not universal.

The paper examines more than aggregate correlation: it reports per-dimension results, cross-model agreement, variability across judges, augmentation/filtering ablations, high- versus low-quality subsets, alternative weighting, binarized-baseline results, and a limited inference-budget control.

The authors provide human studies, costs, model identifiers, seed questions, prompt templates, and a code link. These efforts improve transparency and offer preliminary evidence that humans can apply the checklist protocol.
weaknesses: The central attribution is not identified. CheckEval simultaneously introduces human-designed subdimensions, 20–35 task-specific questions, GPT-4o augmentation/filtering, binary decisions, finer-grained aggregate scores, and substantially more prompt/output computation. G-Eval and SEEval receive a coarse criterion and emit one Likert rating. A matched factorial comparison—decomposed versus holistic crossed with binary versus Likert scoring, using identical rubric content and comparable computation—is necessary. Post-hoc binarization of G-Eval and one n=3 experiment on one model/dataset do not resolve these confounds.

The primary inter-evaluator-agreement analysis is critically under-specified. The paper does not state the unit of analysis, Krippendorff distance level, score discretization, or treatment of checklist aggregation. The identical alpha and kappa values for CheckEval strongly suggest agreement is measured over individual binary question answers, whereas baseline agreement is measured over one holistic rating per example. If so, the comparison does not establish reliability of the final sample-level CheckEval score; if aggregate proportions were used, Fleiss' kappa requires an unexplained categorization. Score-level ICC/concordance, calibration, uncertainty, and variance should be reported on a common output space.

The main empirical claims lack uncertainty estimates or paired significance tests. Many headline improvements are only 0.01–0.03, CheckEval loses for some model/dataset combinations and dimensions, and numerous comparisons are made without multiplicity control. Topical-Chat responses are also nested within conversations, but this dependence is not addressed. Consequently, wording such as “significant” and “consistently” outperforming is not supported.

The human evidence is too limited to validate the broad claims. Correlation uses only 20 stratified SummEval summaries and tests correlation against zero rather than whether systems differ; agreement covers only relevance on one dataset. The claimed approximately 10,000 responses per annotator is inconsistent with 100 summaries times the reported 26 relevance questions, which gives about 2,600. Checklist validation mainly reports the proportion of questions endorsed as acceptable, without a gold standard, rejected-question recall, coverage assessment, or robust chance-corrected agreement.

Reliability is tested for one fixed, author-designed checklist, not across seed-question writers, augmentation/filter models, generated checklist variants, question orderings, paraphrases, or repeated runs. Equal weighting also makes the number of LLM-generated questions an arbitrary implicit weight on each subdimension. The experiments are largely restricted to short outputs from older summarization and dialogue benchmarks, so claims about open-ended text and broader NLG evaluation are premature.

The claimed interpretability is plausible but not demonstrated: Boolean answers identify checklist items, yet provide neither evidence spans nor faithful rationales, and the paper offers only a favorable case study rather than a human interpretability evaluation. Reproducibility is also incomplete in the manuscript because augmentation prompts retain unresolved placeholders, final augmented checklists are absent, the fixed seed and exact GPT snapshots are unspecified, and parsing/failure handling and several dataset sample sizes are not documented. Overall, the end-to-end result is promising and close to Findings level, but the agreement analysis and confounded baseline comparison prevent a sound positive recommendation in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexamined issue: whether LLM-based evaluation is stable across evaluator models. The checklist formulation is simple, relevant to NLP evaluation, and makes individual scoring decisions more traceable than a single holistic rating.

The empirical coverage is substantial: 12 open- and closed-weight evaluators of several sizes are tested on summarization, dialogue, and factual-consistency benchmarks, with detailed per-model and per-dimension results.

CheckEval generally correlates better with benchmark human judgments, particularly for weaker evaluators. The paper also includes human application of the checklist, component ablations, cost information, and analyses of output binarization and inference budget.
The presentation is clear, limitations are discussed candidly, and the paper provides prompts, model and dataset information, and a public code link.
weaknesses: The central inter-evaluator-agreement claim is not adequately validated. CheckEval produces many binary question judgments that are aggregated into a proportion, whereas G-Eval and SEEval produce one ordinal rating. The paper does not clearly specify the unit of analysis and measurement level used for Krippendorff's alpha and Fleiss' kappa. These coefficients depend strongly on label granularity and prevalence, so values from the two protocols are not automatically comparable. Thresholding a holistic Likert rating in Appendix C.3 does not reproduce CheckEval's repeated-question structure. Consequently, the claimed 0.45 agreement improvement does not yet establish greater reliability of the final evaluation scores.

The comparison is confounded by aggregation budget: each CheckEval score averages roughly 20–35 binary decisions, while the baselines use one generation with n=1. Variance reduction is expected from such averaging. The n=3 control covers only one model and dataset and reports correlation rather than agreement; it is not decision- or compute-matched and does not resolve the central confound.

CheckEval bundles manual criterion decomposition, binary output, numerous repeated judgments, LLM augmentation, filtering, and averaging. The ablations do not isolate which component causes the gains, so the causal attribution to checklist decomposition or binary scoring is unsupported.

The main correlation improvements have no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or clustered bootstrap analysis, despite repeated summaries sharing documents and systems. Many gains for strong models are small, and CheckEval loses on several model–dimension combinations, especially Topical-Chat groundedness. The paper's language of 'significant improvements' is therefore unjustified.

Construct validity depends heavily on author-designed sub-dimensions and arbitrary numbers of generated questions, which implicitly weight some attributes more than others. Some seed criteria appear redundant or misaligned—for example, the Topical-Chat groundedness seeds largely assess conversational relevance and consistency rather than grounding in the supplied fact. The complete final checklists are not included, preventing independent assessment of coverage and redundancy.

The human evidence is too limited for the strength of the claims. Correlation is evaluated on only 20 stratified summaries, agreement on only the relevance dimension, and just three expert annotators. The reported human kappa of 0.53 is moderate rather than high, uncertainty intervals are omitted, and checklist-quality agreement is only about 0.63–0.68 under a strongly positive response distribution.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: exact proprietary-model snapshots, checklist-generation decoding settings, filled augmentation conditions/examples, complete generated checklists, parsing and failure-handling rules, and precise agreement computations are not documented in the manuscript. Interpretability is also supported only by one selected case study; binary answers identify contributing items but are not explanations or evidence of faithful reasoning. Overall, these issues undermine the paper's principal reliability claim and prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although a careful reanalysis with matched baselines and stronger validation could make it viable.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexamined issue: evaluator-model consistency, not merely correlation with human scores. The checklist decomposition is simple, intuitive, and diagnostically useful.

Evaluation spans 12 open and proprietary judges of several sizes, two main NLG benchmarks, and an additional QAGS study. Per-model and per-dimension results generally show competitive or improved human correlation.
The paper includes useful ablations and controls involving augmentation, filtering, Likert-score binarization, inference budget, question weighting, and high- versus low-quality outputs.

Human studies examine checklist quality, human–LLM correlation, and agreement. The paper is clearly organized and provides code, model links, seed questions, and prompt templates. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-kfzt5q3y/call-67ede5c5bf8c4e17b60703920adc4e1b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The decisive concern is that the headline inter-evaluator agreement comparison is not demonstrably like-for-like. CheckEval produces 20–35 binary decisions per dimension, whereas G-Eval and SEEval produce one holistic Likert rating. Thresholding the holistic rating does not match the decision granularity or averaging budget. Agreement or dispersion should be reported directly on every method’s final scores, using measures such as ICC and pairwise rank/absolute agreement with uncertainty.

The claim of reduced “score variance” is overstated: Table 15 reports variance of correlations with humans across only 12 models, not variance of scores assigned to the same inputs. Thus neither this analysis nor the reported checklist-level kappa fully establishes stability of the deployed aggregate score.

Headline correlation and IEA differences lack confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Several correlation gains are only 0.01–0.05, yet the paper describes broad or significant improvement without bootstrap tests accounting for dependent correlations and multiple model/dimension comparisons.

Compute is insufficiently controlled. CheckEval obtains over 100 binary judgments per example across dimensions, while the principal baseline obtains one rating per dimension. The n=3 G-Eval control covers only Mistral-Large on Topical-Chat and does not match tokens or decisions, leaving open how much improvement comes from increased inference and averaging redundant questions.

Human validation remains narrow: human–LLM correlation uses only 20 summaries, agreement is tested only for SummEval relevance, and human kappa is a moderate 0.53. The stated workload is also inconsistent: 100 summaries times the 26-question relevance checklist is about 2,600 decisions per annotator, not the reported 10,000.

Generalization and explainability claims exceed the evidence. The main experiments cover summarization and knowledge-grounded dialogue, with QAGS adding another summarization setting; checklists are manually tailored to benchmark definitions and are not tested for transfer. Explainability is supported mainly by one selected case, while binary answers provide traceability but no rationale or fidelity guarantee. The paper’s own checklist-quality validation leaves 15–19% of filtered questions failing the stated criteria.

strengths: Targets an important, underexamined problem: reliability across LLM judges rather than only correlation with human ratings. The checklist mechanism is simple, practical, and more traceable than a single holistic score.

Provides broad empirical coverage across 12 open and proprietary evaluators and three benchmarks involving summarization, dialogue, and factual consistency. CheckEval generally improves human correlation and substantially reduces model-to-model variability, especially for weaker judges.

Includes useful validation and diagnostic work: human application of the checklist, checklist-quality assessment, component ablations, Likert-binarization controls, an inference-budget experiment, weighting analysis, and quality-stratified results.
The presentation is clear and unusually transparent about prompts, hyperparameters, model identifiers, licenses, hardware, and API costs; public code further supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central inter-evaluator-agreement analysis is insufficiently specified and potentially non-comparable. CheckEval produces many question-level binary judgments, whereas G-Eval and SEEval produce one holistic Likert judgment. The paper does not clearly state whether alpha and kappa operate on atomic answers or aggregated example scores, nor the distance/weighting conventions. Thresholding holistic Likert outputs does not remove the granularity and item-content confounds. Agreement or ICC on the final per-example scores is needed to substantiate the headline reliability claim.

The human-correlation comparison confounds decomposition with rubric detail, score resolution, and computation. CheckEval uses 20–35 task-specific questions and up to 200 output tokens, while G-Eval uses a single temperature-zero sample and a discrete score. The limited n=3 control on one model and dataset neither matches CheckEval's decision budget nor fully represents G-Eval's sampling/probability-aggregation variants.

No paired bootstrap tests or confidence intervals establish that CheckEval's correlation and agreement improvements exceed sampling uncertainty. Several differences are small or reverse for particular models and dimensions, notably Topical-Chat groundedness and parts of SummEval, making claims of significant and consistent superiority too strong.

Generalization remains limited because the checklists are manually tailored to two principal tasks, with no held-out task or checklist-transfer experiment. Some displayed seed questions overlap dimensions, penalize valid paraphrases, or are not genuinely atomic. Filtering removes no questions in six of eight dimensions and yields essentially no rounded SummEval ablation gain.

The human evidence is limited: correlation uses only 20 summaries, and agreement is evaluated only for relevance. The stated approximately 10,000 answers per annotator conflicts with 100 summaries times 26 relevance questions, which is about 2,600. Full final checklists, filled prompt fields, exact proprietary-model snapshots, parsing/failure handling, human annotations, and the precise agreement implementation are also absent from the manuscript, although the code link may mitigate some omissions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, well-motivated problem: evaluator reliability across LLM judges rather than human correlation alone. CheckEval is simple, understandable, and directly relevant to NLG evaluation. The reviewed source is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8sum_0zo/call-56a173f690564769a8a3e3920e252341/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The evaluation is unusually broad in judge models: twelve open- and closed-weight LLMs spanning several model families and sizes. Across SummEval and Topical-Chat, CheckEval generally improves human correlation model-by-model rather than succeeding only with a selected judge; the QAGS results provide additional supporting evidence.

The checklist exposes criterion-level decisions, making errors easier to inspect than a single unexplained Likert rating. The staged description—human-defined subdimensions, LLM augmentation and filtering, then binary evaluation—is clear and practically implementable.

The authors examine several plausible alternatives through augmentation/filtering ablations, learned question weighting, binarized G-Eval outputs, a larger inference budget, quality-stratified analysis, and human validation. These analyses materially strengthen the empirical paper.
Reproducibility is aided by the linked code, named model checkpoints, generation settings, seed questions, prompt templates, dataset information, and API-cost estimates.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is that the central inter-evaluator-agreement comparison is not defined on a clearly common outcome. CheckEval produces 20–35 binary decisions per dimension and then averages them into a fractional score, whereas G-Eval and SEEval produce one holistic Likert rating. The near-identical alpha and kappa values for CheckEval suggest agreement was computed over question-level binary answers, but the paper interprets these numbers as agreement of final evaluation scores. Binarizing one holistic G-Eval rating does not match the item structure or repeated judgments of CheckEval. The paper should report agreement directly on each method’s final per-example scores using an appropriate common measure, such as interval Krippendorff alpha, ICC, pairwise rank correlation, or mean absolute judge deviation. Until then, the headline agreement gain of 0.45 is not securely established.

Human-correlation comparisons confound decomposition with inference budget and score resolution. CheckEval averages dozens of decisions, producing a much finer-grained and effectively ensembled score, while the principal baselines use one 3- or 5-level output. The n=3 experiment covers only Mistral-Large on Topical-Chat and neither matches the number of decisions nor isolates resolution, decomposition, and binary response format. A factorial, matched-token/call comparison—including repeated or probability-weighted Likert scoring and the same subcriteria answered on Likert scales—is needed for the causal claims.

The paper repeatedly characterizes improvements as significant but provides no confidence intervals or paired significance tests for the main correlation, agreement, or variance differences. Samples are also nested by source document, system, or conversation, so an item-level test without clustered resampling would be insufficient. Variance and KDE estimates over only twelve heterogeneous judges are descriptive, and “reduced score variance” overstates Table 15, which reports variance of correlations rather than per-example scores.

Checklist construct validity remains uncertain. Question counts vary substantially and uniform averaging therefore gives implicit, LLM-generated weights to frequently paraphrased concepts. Several seeds overlap dimensions or are questionable operationalizations—for example, Topical-Chat groundedness questions largely concern conversational relevance and consistency rather than support from the supplied fact, while SummEval relevance rewards reuse of source terminology. The filtering stage removes almost nothing, and its human validation assesses question acceptability rather than coverage, nonredundancy, or dimensional discriminance.

The direct human validation is too limited to resolve these concerns: correlation uses only 20 summaries, agreement uses 100 summaries for relevance alone, aggregation and statistical units are insufficiently explained, and uncertainty is not reported. Human kappa of 0.53 is moderate rather than clearly high. Moreover, agreement between humans and LLMs applying the same checklist mainly validates compliance with that protocol, not the checklist’s correspondence to the intended quality constructs.

Generality and self-contained reproducibility are limited. The main evidence covers two English, relatively short-form tasks, with QAGS adding another summarization setting; no held-out task tests whether a newly constructed checklist transfers without benchmark-specific iteration. The final augmented checklists, fully instantiated augmentation prompts, exact proprietary model snapshots, construction labor, and matched inference costs are not all reported in the manuscript. Binary labels also provide traceability but not a rationale, so the stronger claim of explainability is not directly evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, highly relevant weakness of LLM-based NLG evaluation: results can depend strongly on the evaluator model. The checklist formulation is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad: 12 open- and closed-source evaluators spanning several model sizes, two main benchmarks, and additional QAGS experiments. CheckEval generally improves correlation with human scores, with particularly convincing gains for several weaker evaluators.

The paper includes useful per-dimension results, ablations, human studies, question-weighting experiments, a binarized-baseline analysis, and an inference-budget check. Prompts, seed questions, model identifiers, implementation details, and a code link also improve transparency.

Binary responses expose which criteria contributed to a score, providing more diagnostic information than a single holistic rating, even though the broader interpretability claim remains insufficiently validated.
weaknesses: The central inter-evaluator-agreement comparison is not adequately specified or demonstrably comparable. CheckEval appears to compute agreement over individual binary question responses, whereas G-Eval and SEEval are assessed using one holistic Likert rating per text. Thus the methods differ simultaneously in evaluation unit, number and prevalence of categories, granularity, and number of decisions. Binarizing the holistic baselines does not resolve the unit mismatch. Agreement or error between final normalized scores—using an appropriate ICC, interval alpha, pairwise correlation, or MAE—is needed before concluding that CheckEval produces more consistent scores.

The headline claim of improving average agreement “by 0.45” is not clearly recoverable from the reported tables. Moreover, the reported stability variance is variance among 12 correlation coefficients, not variance of evaluation scores as the abstract suggests. These distinctions materially affect the paper's main reliability claim.

The main correlation and agreement comparisons lack confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Several gains are small, raw correlations are averaged across dimensions without Fisher transformation, and the method-specific post-hoc selection of different “Top-3” evaluator sets makes those agreement comparisons especially difficult to interpret.

Checklist construction creates unresolved validity and weighting issues. Different numbers of augmented questions implicitly give sub-dimensions different weights, and several seed criteria overlap across dimensions or poorly operationalize the target construct—for example, the Topical-Chat groundedness questions do not directly test consistency with the supplied grounding fact. The complete final checklists and sufficiently exact augmentation details are not included in the manuscript itself.

The human evidence is too limited to close these concerns: the correlation study uses only 20 summaries; agreement is evaluated on only relevance; kappa values of 0.53 for humans and 0.49 for humans plus LLMs are moderate and reported without intervals; and the stated approximately 10,000 answers per annotator is inconsistent with 100 summaries times the reported 26 relevance questions. Checklist filtering is assessed mainly on retained items rather than both retained and removed items.

CheckEval elicits 20–35 judgments per dimension, while the principal baselines usually produce one holistic judgment. The three-sample budget experiment covers only one model and dataset and does not genuinely equalize computation or decision opportunities. A comparably decomposed baseline or systematic matched-budget evaluation is needed.

Evidence for interpretability consists mainly of the transparent output format and a selected case study; no human evaluation establishes that users can understand, diagnose, or trust CheckEval decisions better. Generalization is also demonstrated only for summarization, dialogue response evaluation, and factual consistency benchmarks.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexamined problem: robustness to the choice of LLM judge, considered separately from correlation with human ratings.
The checklist framework is simple, task-relevant, and more transparent than a single holistic score because individual quality criteria can be inspected.

The empirical sweep is substantial: 12 open and proprietary evaluator models, consistent backbone-level comparisons, two main benchmarks, and additional QAGS results. CheckEval generally improves human correlation, particularly for weaker judges.

Human studies, component ablations, quality-stratified analyses, prompts, model identifiers, seed questions, question counts, costs, and a code link provide useful supporting material. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges task-specific construction and weaknesses of binary judgments. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-eh2nkdj7/call-ea9d8e893a214cff8c79d24a9b690bdb/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central claimed 0.45 agreement improvement is not auditable as a like-for-like comparison. The paper does not specify the agreement unit, Krippendorff distance function, or treatment of aggregated checklist scores. CheckEval's alpha and kappa values are identical throughout, suggesting agreement may be calculated over individual binary question responses, whereas baseline agreement concerns one text-level Likert rating. This would compare text-question decisions against final text scores rather than measuring reliability of each method's final output. Binarizing G-Eval does not resolve that granularity mismatch.

The abstract claims reduced score variance, but Table 15 reports variance of correlations across only 12 models, not variance of scores assigned to the same examples. With one deterministic run per model, the paper also provides no test-retest evidence. The broader reliability claims should therefore be narrowed substantially.

Statistical support for comparative claims is inadequate. There are no paired bootstrap confidence intervals or tests for differences between methods, although many gains for strong models are very small or dimension-dependent. Reported p-values only establish that selected correlations differ from zero. Raw correlation coefficients are averaged directly, and the post-hoc Top-3 comparison uses different model sets for different methods.

The comparison confounds protocol design with inference budget and supervision. CheckEval elicits roughly 20–35 decisions per dimension with up to 200 output tokens, while G-Eval produces one rating with 20 tokens. The n=3 control covers only Mistral-Large on Topical-Chat and remains far from a matched decision or token budget; no systematic cost or latency comparison is given.

Uniformly averaging questions implicitly weights sub-dimensions according to how many variants GPT-4o happened to generate. Residual redundancy can further overweight particular properties. Some seed criteria also appear misaligned—for example, Topical-Chat groundedness is operationalized largely through conversational relevance and consistency rather than explicit support from the supplied fact.

External validity is limited. Checklist construction and analysis use the same established benchmarks, and QAGS adds another summarization-factuality setting rather than a substantially new task. There is no held-out task showing that the human-designed and GPT-augmented construction procedure transfers without benchmark-specific tuning.

The human evidence is too narrow to settle these concerns: protocol correlation uses only 20 summaries; agreement uses three expert annotators and only relevance; reported kappa values of 0.53 for humans and 0.49 for humans plus LLMs are moderate rather than clearly high; and no confidence intervals are supplied. The checklist-quality study assesses acceptability of retained questions but not rejected questions or overall criterion coverage.

Although many reproducibility details are supplied, exact proprietary-model snapshots, the random seed, output parsing and failure handling, and the complete generated checklists are absent from the manuscript. Given the unresolved validity of the headline agreement analysis, the work is presently just below the soundness threshold for Findings, though the existing experimental base makes it a close and repairable case.
